solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: River on Henri's land full of fish, a variable earner

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it

parts.note: Henri is a typical French name, so his land is France
an eel is a fish; it goes inside FRANCE after FR
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A French river runs through land teeming with fish, somehow linked to a worker with unpredictable pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River' comes first in the clue but its R lands last: 'on' places it after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A freelancer works for many clients rather than on a salary, so earnings vary from month to month.

clue.text: Signal ship must show to port Spooner's shown to starboard

definitions.text: Signal ship must show to port

indicators.note: Rev. Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds of the two words are exchanged

parts.note: led, as in led the way, i.e. shown
starboard is the right-hand side of a ship
swap the L and R sounds

explanation.surface: A rule of the sea: which navigation light a ship displays on the left and which on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on a real rule: ships carry a red light on the port side and a green one to starboard, so the clue neatly pairs port with its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's port side carries a red navigation light, a signal to other vessels of its heading.

clue.text: Energy doubled self-confidence

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
energy again, this time as go, as in full of get-up-and-go

explanation.surface: Doubling your energy boosts your self-belief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubled' is not a repeat of the same letters: energy is given twice in two different forms, E and GO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ego is one's sense of self-worth, which can mean self-confidence.

clue.text: Grant's off in Scotland with doctor, heading north

parts.note: awa is Scots for away, i.e. off

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor, reversed here

explanation.surface: Someone called Grant has gone off to Scotland with a doctor, heading up north.
explanation.walkthrough: Grant looks like a man's name, but it is the definition, a noun meaning something given; the ’s just means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An award is a grant, a sum formally given, as in a research grant.

clue.text: Sort of bun beside tea cups

indicators.note: to cup something is to hold it in cupped hands

parts.note: cha (char) is British slang for tea
beside in the sense of besides, i.e. else

explanation.surface: A kind of bun is served next to some teacups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea cups' reads as teacups, but 'cups' is a verb: CHA holds ELSE. A Chelsea bun is a spiral currant bun, a British teatime staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A Chelsea bun is a sticky rolled currant bun named after the London district.

clue.text: Motors with limited range burn out as modelled

indicators.note: clay that is modelled is shaped into a new form

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Short-range cars burn out as a design flaw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Motors' and 'burn out' make one car story, but 'burn out as' is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A runabout is a small car for short local trips, so its range is limited.

clue.text: Large book showing selfish dedication?

definitions.meaning: a weighty volume, the more literary word for a big book
split in two, the word reads as a book inscription naming the author themself

explanation.surface: A fat volume whose author dedicated it to themself.
explanation.walkthrough: Split TOME as TO ME and it becomes the dedication of an author with no one else to thank.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a large, scholarly volume; the second sense splits the word into a dedication of the book to its own writer.

clue.text: Computer blitzed nine second game

indicators.note: something blitzed is smashed up, so NINE is rearranged

parts.note: a tablet is a handheld computer
NINE rearranged
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: A computer thrashed nine opponents in a second game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second game' reads as a rematch, but 'second' is only S and 'game' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Table tennis, or ping-pong, is a game played with bats and a light ball over a net.

clue.text: A girl, not yet twelve, set up resort

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised, so the letters read upwards

parts.note: as written
gal is informal for girl
before noon is a.m.

explanation.surface: A young girl, still under twelve, organises a trip to a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not yet twelve' suggests a child's age; it is the time of day, before twelve noon, i.e. AM.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaga is a resort city on Spain's Costa del Sol.

clue.text: Cause promoter fuss with a VAT code

indicators.note: to fuss with something is to fiddle with it, moving the letters about

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Someone stirs up trouble over a tax code, as in a dispute about VAT.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cause promoter fuss' reads as one who causes a promoter trouble, but the definition is 'Cause promoter', one who promotes a cause.
explanation.definitionFit: An advocate publicly supports or promotes a cause.

clue.text: Illicit delivery which Cinderella expected, initially?

definitions.meaning: in cricket, a delivery is a ball bowled; one that breaks the bowling rules is penalised
before her fairy godmother appeared, Cinderella was told she would not be going to the prince’s dance

explanation.surface: A package that shouldn't have been sent, which Cinderella was waiting for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' is not a first-letter signal: it means at the start of the story, before her fairy godmother stepped in. In cricket, a delivery is a ball bowled.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-ball is a cricket delivery that breaks the rules, so the batting side gets a penalty run.

clue.text: A bit of fish sent back, given meal stank

indicators.note: something sent back goes the other way

parts.note: a fin is part of a fish, reversed here
someone given a meal has been fed

explanation.surface: A diner sends back a bit of fish, having been served a meal that smelt off.
explanation.walkthrough: The restaurant scene makes 'sent back' a complaint; it only turns FIN round. Niff is British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: To niff is British slang for to smell bad, so niffed means stank.

clue.text: Oscar winner as relaxation quietly eats chewy sweet

parts.note: as in 'as a reason', i.e. for
rest is relaxation
chewing gum; it sits inside REST P
P is piano, the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: A film star relaxes by quietly chewing a sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar winner' suggests an actor; here it is a film. Also, 'as' is not a link word but gives FOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Forrest Gump won the 1995 Academy Award for Best Picture.

clue.text: Plastic beer mugs in sink

indicators.note: something plastic can be moulded into any shape

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Plastic pint glasses have been left in the kitchen sink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like the kitchen sink, a noun; it is the verb, to put under water.
explanation.definitionFit: To submerge something is to sink it beneath the surface of water.

clue.text: Insufficient amount from a Thermos, cast agreed

indicators.note: something cast is thrown or moulded anew, so A THERMOS is rearranged

parts.note: A THERMOS rearranged
'Sure!' is a way of saying you agree

explanation.surface: A flask doesn't hold enough tea, and everyone is in agreement about it.
explanation.walkthrough: A Thermos is a vacuum flask; its name is here only for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Short measure is less than the amount paid for, as with a pint poured short.

clue.text: Ill relation of Mike lives on wine

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
lives in the sense of exists, is
re means on or about
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: A sickly relative called Mike survives on a diet of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill relation' paints a sick relative; it means a bad account, relation in its sense of a telling.
explanation.definitionFit: A misreport is an inaccurate account, relation meaning a narration and ill meaning badly done.

clue.text: Large mammal that's vanished mother never spots returning

parts.note: ma is informal for mother

indicators.note: going back, so NO DOTS reads upwards in this down clue

parts.note: no dots, i.e. never any spots, reversed here

explanation.surface: A mother who has disappeared is never seen coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' reads as a verb, sees; it is a noun, dots, and 'never' gives NO.
explanation.definitionFit: The mastodon was a large elephant-like mammal that is now extinct.

clue.text: Time late riser's appearance is noted in church?

definitions.text: Time late riser's appearance is noted in church?

parts.note: the surface suggests someone who sleeps in turning up at last; the setter means Christ, rising from the dead after the crucifixion
the definition is a point in the calendar: the day on which that rising is marked in church

explanation.surface: A lie-in-lover's arrival at church is remarked upon by the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late riser' suggests someone who sleeps in; it is Christ, risen after death, and the day of the Resurrection is marked in church.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter Sunday is the day Christians celebrate Christ's rising from the dead.

clue.text: Awful leech attached to tier of organisation

indicators.note: an awful version of LEECH is a mangled one

parts.note: LEECH rearranged
on as in stuck on, attached

explanation.surface: A dreadful bloodsucker clings to a level of management.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attached to' does double duty here: it means on, which gives ON, and places it after the leech.
explanation.definitionFit: An echelon is a level or rank in an organisation, as in the upper echelons.

clue.text: Speedos serve to cover bum

indicators.note: the two words cover the answer, holding it inside

parts.note: speeDOS SERve

explanation.surface: Tight swimming trunks do the job of covering your backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' means backside in the picture; the definition uses its other sense, a tramp. Speedos are brief swimming trunks.
explanation.definitionFit: A dosser is British slang for a homeless person or idler, a bum.

clue.text: Anniversary couple keep hotel robes

parts.note: a keep is a castle's stronghold, a fort
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to couple is to tie together; it goes inside FORTH

explanation.surface: A pair celebrating a wedding anniversary stay on at a hotel in bathrobes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' and 'Anniversary' set up a married pair, but couple is a verb, tie, and 'robes' clothes it in FORTH.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortieth is a fortieth anniversary, as in 'their fortieth', the ruby wedding.

clue.text: Best school gymnasts possibly tender no longer

parts.note: physical education, the school lesson for gymnasts
a set is a teaching group in a British school
A is the top grade

explanation.surface: The top school gymnastics team is perhaps no longer so gentle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like an adjective, soft; it is legal tender, money, and the peseta was Spain's currency until the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: The peseta was Spain's legal tender until it was replaced by the euro in 2002.

clue.text: Notice fuzz from beneath furry forest creature

indicators.note: in a down clue, reading from beneath means reading upwards

parts.note: an ad is a notice, an advertisement
nap is the fuzzy surface of cloth

explanation.surface: Someone spots fuzz under a furry woodland animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuzz' may suggest police slang; here it is the nap on fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant panda is a furry black-and-white bear living in China's bamboo forests.

clue.text: Bogus note written after signing off party in Brussels?

parts.note: a postscript, added after the signature
Brussels is the seat of the European Union
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A fake note is added after the signature by someone at a Brussels party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party in Brussels' suggests a political party; it is an EU do, a party held in Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Pseudo means sham or bogus, not genuine.

clue.text: Publican emptied leaky bottles with son

indicators.note: an emptied word loses its middle, leaving the outer letters

parts.note: leaky with its middle removed
with means and
a lad is a son or boy

explanation.surface: A pub owner emptied the leaky bottles together with her son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a noun, the pub's stock; it is a verb meaning holds, and 'emptied' strips a word to its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a publican is whoever keeps a pub, and in Britain a woman doing so is called the landlady.

clue.text: Somewhere to go for a game of cards

definitions.meaning: 'go' is the euphemism: the place you go when nature calls, in British slang
an old gambling card game, popular in the 17th and 18th centuries

explanation.surface: A place to head for an evening of card-playing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhere to go' sounds like a destination; 'go' is the euphemism, so it is the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Loo is the British word for toilet, and also an old gambling card game.

clue.text: A page turned over for homework

parts.note: a as in 'a day', i.e. per
P is the abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A page is turned over to start on schoolwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' seems a mere article; it means per, as in 'twice a week'. Prep is British school slang for homework.
explanation.definitionFit: Prep, short for preparation, is homework in British schools, especially boarding schools.

clue.text: Essentially identical straw regularly eaten by brown horse

parts.note: tan is a light brown
the second and fourth letters of straw
a mount is a horse for riding

explanation.surface: A brown horse munches straw, much the same as any other.
explanation.walkthrough: The straw really would be eaten by a horse, but 'regularly' means only every other letter of it goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Tantamount means equivalent in effect, as in 'tantamount to a confession'.
